name: bourdon

builder: footage 16 (sound_changes={'footage': 16.0} on stopped diapason's _pipe_stop(STOPPED_FLUTE_LEVELS, chiff=0.02)); the footage is sourced (the Encyclopedia of Organ Stops), nothing else changes
notes: Sound-alike: the Encyclopedia of Organ Stops (Edward L. Stauff; raw HTML, its Windows-1252 bytes saved as UTF-8 in build/batch-13-pages/bourdon--2.txt): 'A 16' stopped wooden flute of large scale.' 'It is possibly the single most common 16' pedal stop.' 'It is similar to, and occasionally synonymous with, the Gedeckt and the Stopped Diapason.' The entry's bibliography cites Audsley, Grove, Irwin, Wedgwood and others. Audsley, Organ-Stops and Their Artistic Registration (1921, public domain; its archive.org text https://archive.org/download/cu31924086010331/cu31924086010331_djvu.txt, saved as bourdon--3.txt), BOURDON: 'In English and American Organs the Bourdon may be said to invariably appear in the form of a covered, labial wood stop, of large scale and 16 ft. pitch.' 'Blown by wind of moderate pressure, these stops yield tones in which the twelfth, or first har- monic of a stopped pipe, is more or less prominent' and 'it is certain the stop belongs to the flute-work of the Organ.' Audsley, The Organ of the Twentieth Century (1919, public domain; its archive.org text https://archive.org/download/organoftwentieth00audsuoft/organoftwentieth00audsuoft_djvu.txt, saved as bourdon--4.txt): 'Covered pipes cannot give the uneven upper partial tones, such as the first or octave and the third or super-octave, etc.' (Audsley counts upper partials from the octave, so his 'uneven upper partials' are harmonics 2 and 4, the even harmonics) and 'The most important covered wood stops are the STOPPED DIAPASON, BOURDON, DOPPELFLOTE, LIEBLICHGEDECKT, and QUINTATEN.' So the bourdon is a stopped flue with the stopped diapason's cited trait (the missing even harmonics), and stopped diapason (this half's SHIP, STOPPED_FLUTE_LEVELS at 8') is its nearest entry: the same stopped flute family, an octave lower (the footage ruling's rule 3). The Bourdon (organ pipe) page (bourdon--5.txt) says the stopper 'also eliminates the development of even-numbered [[harmonic]]s', but the line is uncited (a {{One source}} page whose only source is the Encyclopedia), so it decides nothing. The parent, stopped diapason, is a SHIP row of this half (C2-C7, 8'). Rule 7: the only difference from stopped diapason is the footage, which is pitch (the footage ruling's rule 3), so SOUND_ALIKE with footage 16. Range: the stop's division is the pedal. Audsley, BOURDON: «The Bourdon, 16 ft., most frequently appears, in English and .A.merican instruments of moderate dimensions, in the Pedal Organ;» the Encyclopedia: «It is possibly the single most common 16' pedal stop.» (Audsley's manual Bourdons are German and French, of 32 ft., 16 ft. or 8 ft., and the Encyclopedia's 16' is the pedal form; the controller's ruling, fix round 1.) The pedal's compass: the AGO's Standard Console Guidelines, as Organ Supply Industries' console brochure reproduces them (https://www.organsupply.com/assets/Brochures/Console-Tri-Fold.pdf, fetched, its text saved as build/batch-13-pages/bourdon--7.txt), under Pedalboard: «Compass: 32 notes, CCC to G» and, under Manuals, «Compass: CC to c4, 61 notes.» The manual line fixes the notation (organ builders' CC, the manual's lowest key at 8' pitch, is C2, and c4 is C7), so CCC to G is C1-G3, 32 notes (C1 + 31 semitones = G3): the pedal written at its 16' unison, an octave below its keys. The AGO's Pipe Organ Guide (archived, https://web.archive.org/web/20070927154656/http://www.agohq.org/guide/pages/pages_5_5/frameset01.html, its frame saved as bourdon--6.txt) gives the keys as written: «Pedal keyboards are also different lengths, but low C is also the lowest written note.» «Some have 30 notes-to F above middle C; others have 32-to G above middle C.» The standard is the 32-note board (the guidelines; range ruling 6), so its keys at 8' pitch are C2 (low C) to G4 (G above middle C), 32 keys, the same board as CCC to G at 16'. Lowest C2, highest G4, inside A0-C8. Footage: the Encyclopedia of Organ Stops: «A 16' stopped wooden flute of large scale.» Audsley gives the same pitch («covered, labial wood stop, of large scale and 16 ft. pitch») and calls the 8' and 32' forms occasional. Footage 16. A 16' stop sounds an octave below its keys: C2-G4 at 8' pitch sound C1-G3, inside A0-C8 (the footage ruling's rule 6).

notes: Encyclopedia of Organ Stops (raw HTML, its Windows-1252 bytes saved as UTF-8 in build/batch-13-pages/cornet-organ--2.txt): 'In its quintessential form, the Cornet is a wide-scaled compound stop without breaks, containing a third-sounding rank, often of short (treble) compass.' notes: The audit marked it '(existence and range) UNVERIFIED'; rule 6: its own page, fetched. Encyclopedia of Organ Stops, Diaphone (it lists 'Diaphonic Diapason' as an English name of the stop; raw HTML saved as UTF-8 in build/batch-13-pages/diaphonic-diapason--1.txt): 'Wind-blown organ pipes come in two broad types: flues and reeds. While the Diaphone is in many ways similar to reeds, it is considered to be in a class by itself, sometimes called "valvular". Instead of a reed, it employs a beating palette to produce the vibrations which are amplified and fixed in frequency by a resonator. Unlike beating reeds, the pitch of a Diaphone is not affected by variations in wind pressure.' 'Diaphones are uncommon, and are found most often in theatre organs. Diaphonic pipes are typically only used in the 16' and 32' octaves.' Audsley, Organ-Stops and Their Artistic Registration (1921, public domain; its archive.org text https://archive.org/download/cu31924086010331/cu31924086010331_djvu.txt, saved as diaphonic-diapason--2.txt), DIAPHONE: 'The tone of the Diaphone pipe is created by pulses or vibrations generated in its resonator by the rapid motions of a pallet actuated by compressed air' and 'it is almost im- possible to secure uniformity throughout even the short compass of the Pedal Organ.' So the stop exists, but its sound is a valve's pulses in a resonator, neither a flue's nor a reed's: a cited trait no organ builder makes (rule 4). Its footage is also unsourced as one value ('the 16' and 32' octaves', and Audsley's Worcester and McEwan Hall Diaphones 'could be drawn of 32 ft. and 16 ft. pitch'), and its compass is not stated.
